title: Quality checks: errors to correct, events to keep

explain.prompt: Your checks flag two observations. For each one, explain in 2–3 sentences why you classify it as an error to correct or as a genuine market event to keep, using the other benchmarks on the same day. Why is a rolling **median** of the **previous** days a better reference than the full-sample mean?
rubric: 2021-03-15, Brent 549.70: ten times its recent level while WTI (52.69) and Dubai (52.54) are normal and Brent is back to normal the next day — a shifted decimal point. Error: set to NaN (or replace from a second source), and log the correction.

2020-04-20, WTI −35.90: impossible for Brent or Dubai, but WTI's front-month contract really can go negative at expiry when storage is full; Brent stayed positive (19.06) and the following day WTI is back to a positive level. Genuine event: keep it, document it, and handle it explicitly in later analysis.

The reference must use only past values (shift(1)): checking a value against a level that already includes it, or includes the future, either hides the error or uses information you would not have had.
A median is robust: one bad print does not move it, whereas a mean (and a standard deviation) is contaminated by the very outlier you are looking for.
Rules are per series and economically motivated (Brent/Dubai cannot be negative, WTI can): a blanket 'drop non-positive prices' would delete a real market event.
